directions: There are 10 questions about what you explored, from differentiation to convection currents. Answer every question, and then submit.

displayedOptions.text: They were the hottest materials on young Earth
They were more dense than the other materials
Earth's magnetic field pulled them to the center

items.feedback: Differentiation sorted the melted Earth by density. Iron and nickel were more dense than the other materials, so they sank to the center and formed the core. Lighter materials rose and formed the mantle and crust.

omittedOptions.rationale: "They cooled and hardened before the other materials" rests on an order-of-cooling idea the lesson never develops, so it is the least plausible lure. "Hottest" (confusing temperature with density) and "magnetic field" (thinking the iron core was pulled in by magnetism) keep the two meaningful misconceptions.

items.stem: Long ago, Earth was molten, or melted. Iron and nickel sank to the center. This sorting is called differentiation. Why did these metals sink?

displayedOptions.text: Crust, mantle, outer core, inner core
Crust, outer core, mantle, inner core
Crust, mantle, inner core, outer core

items.feedback: From the surface to the center, the layers are the crust, the mantle, the outer core, and the inner core. Each layer is deeper, hotter, and more dense than the one above it.

omittedOptions.rationale: "Mantle, crust, outer core, inner core" puts the mantle at the surface, which contradicts the most familiar fact in the lesson (we live on the crust), so it is the least plausible. The mantle placed below the outer core, and the two core layers swapped, keep the two ordering errors students actually make.

items.stem: Start at the surface and go to the center. Which list shows Earth's four main layers in order?

displayedOptions.text: It is a thick layer of hot rock that flows slowly
It is a liquid layer made of iron and nickel
It is thin, brittle rock and the least dense layer

items.feedback: The crust is the thin outer layer. It is made of brittle rock, which breaks easily. It is also the least dense layer. The other choices describe the mantle and the outer core.

omittedOptions.rationale: "A solid ball of metal and the densest layer" describes the inner core with words ("ball", "densest") that directly contradict a thin outer layer, so it is the easiest to reject. The mantle description and the outer-core description keep the two nearest layer confusions.

items.stem: Which sentence best describes the crust?

displayedOptions.text: Continental crust, because it is thicker
Oceanic crust, because it is more dense
Oceanic crust, because it is less dense

items.feedback: Oceanic crust is more dense than continental crust. So where they meet, the heavier oceanic crust tends to sink under the lighter continental crust.

omittedOptions.rationale: "Continental crust, because it is more dense" repeats the reversed-density error that "Oceanic crust, because it is less dense" already tests. Keeping the oceanic version leaves two "Oceanic crust" choices, so naming oceanic crust alone never reveals the answer; the student must know why. "Thicker" keeps the thickness-means-heavier misconception.

items.stem: Oceanic crust and continental crust can meet. Then one of them usually sinks under the other. Which one sinks, and why?

displayedOptions.text: It is melted rock, or magma, that moves like a liquid
It is solid rock that stays perfectly still
It is solid rock that can slowly flow

items.feedback: The mantle is solid rock, not liquid magma. Temperature differences let this solid rock flow very slowly, like toothpaste squeezed through a tube. The liquid metal layer is the outer core.

omittedOptions.rationale: "Liquid metal that creates Earth's magnetic field" describes the outer core, a layer-composition confusion that q3 and q8 already probe. Keeping "liquid magma" and "stays perfectly still" means the answer requires knowing the mantle is both solid and slowly flowing.

items.stem: Which sentence best describes the rock in Earth's mantle?

displayedOptions.text: The lithosphere is stiff and broken into plates. The asthenosphere below it flows slowly.
The asthenosphere is stiff and broken into plates. The lithosphere below it flows slowly.
The lithosphere is the whole mantle. The asthenosphere is the crust above it.

items.feedback: The lithosphere is the stiff outer part of Earth. It is made of the crust and the upper mantle, and it is broken into plates. The asthenosphere is just below it, in the upper mantle. It slowly flows.

omittedOptions.rationale: Calling the lithosphere just "the crust" and placing the asthenosphere in "the liquid outer core" is far from anything the lesson teaches and is easy to reject. The swapped layers and the mantle-and-crust confusion keep the two meaningful misconceptions about where these zones are and how they behave.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly compares the lithosphere and the asthenosphere?

displayedOptions.text: It is more dense than the cooler rock above it
It is less dense than the cooler rock above it
It melted into liquid magma that bubbles up

items.feedback: Hot rock near the bottom of the mantle is less dense than the cooler rock above it, so it rises. Near the top, the rock cools, becomes more dense, and sinks again. This loop is a convection current.

omittedOptions.rationale: The magnetic field plays no part in the lesson's convection model, so "Earth's magnetic field pushes it" is the least plausible lure. Reversed density ("more dense") and melting into magma keep the two meaningful misconceptions about why hot rock rises.

items.stem: In a convection current in the mantle, why does hot rock rise?

displayedOptions.text: Pressure from above keeps its metal from melting
It is less dense than the outer core
Earth's magnetic field holds its metal in place

items.feedback: Both parts of the core are iron and nickel. The inner core is hotter. But the crushing pressure from every layer above squeezes its metal so tightly that it cannot become liquid.

omittedOptions.rationale: "It is made of rock instead of metal" contradicts the lesson's repeated statement that the core is iron and nickel, rather than engaging the pressure idea being assessed. A density explanation and the magnetic field (which the lesson ties to the core) keep the two plausible wrong explanations.

items.stem: The inner core is even hotter than the outer core. So why is the inner core solid, while the outer core is liquid?

displayedOptions.text: Magma rises there and erupts from a new volcano
The plates melt together and stop moving
Released energy shakes the crust as an earthquake

items.feedback: When stuck plates suddenly slip, the pressure that built up is released as energy. That energy shakes the crust. The shaking is an earthquake.

omittedOptions.rationale: No link between slipping plates and the magnetic field is taught, so "the magnetic field suddenly reverses" is the least plausible lure. Confusing an earthquake with a volcano, and thinking the plates fuse and stop, keep the two meaningful misconceptions.

items.stem: Two plates are stuck. Pressure builds up along their edges. What happens when the plates suddenly slip?

displayedOptions.text: Plates move on their own first. Their motion heats the mantle. Then the hot mantle causes earthquakes and volcanoes.
Heat drives convection in the mantle. The mantle moves the plates. Moving plates cause earthquakes and volcanoes.
Heat melts the whole mantle into magma. The magma causes earthquakes and volcanoes.

items.feedback: Heat inside Earth makes hot rock less dense, so it rises and drives convection currents in the mantle. The flowing mantle drags the plates. Moving plates cause earthquakes and volcanoes at the surface.

omittedOptions.rationale: "Earth's magnetic field moves the plates" names a driver the lesson never connects to plate motion, so it is the least plausible. The reversed chain (plates first) and the melted-mantle chain keep the two meaningful misconceptions about cause and effect.

items.stem: Which chain of events best explains how Earth's inner layers cause earthquakes and volcanoes at the surface?

showYourThinking.modelAnswer: Earth's core is extremely hot, and that heat rises into the mantle. The mantle is solid rock, but it flows slowly. Hot rock is less dense, so it rises. Cooler rock is more dense, so it sinks. This loop of rising and sinking rock is called convection. Convection currents drag the plates on top, so the plates move. Moving plates can get stuck, and pressure builds up. When they suddenly slip, the energy shakes the crust as an earthquake. In some places where plates meet or pull apart, rock deep below melts into magma, or molten rock. The magma can rise and erupt from volcanoes. If your steps go from the hot core to mantle convection to plate motion to surface change, you have it.
showYourThinking.prompt: Explain how Earth's inner layers cause earthquakes and volcanoes at the surface. Write one or two sentences. Name the steps in order, starting with the hot core. Do not just list the layers. Use the word convection.
